subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Proteins
bigPicture: 20 amino acids in any order and any length give almost unlimited proteins. The sequence decides the folding, and the folding decides the function.

keyIdeas.cue: Describe the general structure of an amino acid.
keyIdeas.answer: A central (alpha) carbon bonded to an amine group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable R-group. You need to recognise it, not draw it.
Condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the next forms a peptide bond and releases water. Word equation: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water.

keyIdeas.cue: Essential vs non-essential amino acids, and why vegans must plan?
keyIdeas.answer: Essential amino acids can't be made by the body and must come from food. Non-essential ones can be made from other amino acids. Single plant foods may be low in some essential amino acids, so vegans combine sources.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is the variety of polypeptides effectively infinite?
keyIdeas.answer: 20 amino acids are coded for, chains can be any length (a few to thousands) and in any order, so there are 20ⁿ possible sequences for n amino acids.

keyIdeas.cue: How do pH and temperature affect proteins?
keyIdeas.answer: High temperature breaks the weak bonds holding the 3D shape. pH changes alter the charges on R-groups, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds. Either can cause denaturation, a loss of shape and function that is usually permanent.
R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic. Hydrophilic ones are polar or charged (acidic or basic). Their properties decide how the chain folds and what it does.

keyIdeas.cue: How does primary structure determine conformation?
keyIdeas.answer: The exact sequence and position of each amino acid decide how the chain folds. So a protein has a precise, repeatable 3D shape, and one change can alter it.

keyIdeas.cue: What are secondary structures and what holds them?
keyIdeas.answer: α-helices and β-pleated sheets, stabilised by hydrogen bonds at regular intervals between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
Hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds (between R-groups made charged by gaining or losing H⁺), disulfide covalent bonds (between two cysteines) and hydrophobic interactions.

keyIdeas.cue: How do polar and non-polar amino acids position themselves?
keyIdeas.answer: In soluble globular proteins, hydrophobic amino acids cluster in the core and hydrophilic ones face the water. Integral membrane proteins have hydrophobic regions that sit in the bilayer.

keyIdeas.cue: What is quaternary structure? Conjugated vs non-conjugated?
keyIdeas.answer: More than one polypeptide chain combined. Non-conjugated: only polypeptides (insulin, collagen). Conjugated: includes a non-polypeptide part, e.g. haemoglobin with four haem groups. Cryo-electron microscopy can image single protein molecules.

keyIdeas.cue: How do globular and fibrous shapes fit function?
keyIdeas.answer: Globular proteins are rounded, often soluble and have a precise binding shape. Insulin binds its receptor. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and strong. Collagen's triple helix gives tensile strength in skin, tendons and bone.

Loss of a protein's 3D shape (and function) without breaking peptide bonds.
Covalent S–S bond between two cysteine R-groups.
Protein with a non-polypeptide component, e.g. haem in haemoglobin.

misconceptions.right: It breaks the weaker bonds holding the shape. The primary sequence is unchanged.
Primary structure is just the sequence. Hydrogen bonds hold secondary (and some tertiary) structure.
Only those made of more than one chain or with a prosthetic group.

misconceptions.wrong: Essential amino acids are the important ones.
misconceptions.right: 'Essential' only means they must be eaten.
